data_source.archive: MAST archive, free, no key required

steps.title: Download
steps.body: Pull light curves for a target from the MAST archive with the lightkurve package. The validation used 4 TESS sectors of TOI 700 (62,074 cadences). The batch scan used 2 sectors per target.

steps.title: Detrend
steps.body: Remove the slow drift in a star's brightness with a Savitzky-Golay filter and drop outlier points. This leaves the short, sharp dips that a transiting planet would cause.

steps.title: Search with Box Least Squares
steps.body: Box Least Squares (BLS) in astropy tests thousands of candidate periods and looks for a repeating box-shaped dip. The validation searched 1 to 40 days; the batch scan searched 0.5 to 30 days. The strongest periodogram spike is the reported signal.

steps.title: Fold and plot
steps.body: Fold the light curve on the best period so all the dips stack on top of each other at phase zero, and plot it. A real transit shows up as a clear dip; noise does not.

limitations: False positives dominate. BLS cannot tell a planet from an eclipsing binary, a background blended binary, starspot modulation, or instrument systematics. TOI 1338 is the textbook case: the strongest signal is the host stars eclipsing each other.
Only the strongest signal per target is reported. Real systems are multi-planet; this pipeline is blind to everything after the first hit.
Only 2 sectors per target were scanned (the validation used 4). Longer baselines find longer periods and beat down noise.
No vetting tests were done: no odd/even transit depth comparison, no secondary eclipse search, no centroid shift check, no transit shape fitting.
BLS is a box model. Real transits are limb-darkened U shapes; the Transit Least Squares (TLS) algorithm is more sensitive, especially for small planets.

This does not beat NASA's ExoMiner++. ExoMiner++ is a deep-learning classifier trained on Kepler plus TESS data that identified about 7,000 TESS candidates (NASA Ames, January 2026), with false-positive rejection built in. This pipeline is a single classical algorithm with no learned vetting. Its value is as an independent, explainable check, not as a competitor.
The batch scan searched periods up to 30 days only, so longer-period planets (such as TOI 1338 b at about 95 days) cannot be found by it.
roadmap: Cross-match every signal against the NASA Exoplanet Archive and the ExoMiner++ candidate list before calling anything interesting.
Add vetting: odd/even depth test, secondary eclipse search, transit shape (V vs U), centroid offsets, and a check against known eclipsing-binary catalogs.
Swap BLS for TLS for small-planet sensitivity.
Stitch all available sectors per target instead of 2.
Cross-check ambiguous signals on Planet Hunters TESS, where human eyes still beat algorithms on long-period and odd-shaped transits.
Submit interesting survivors to ExoFOP (the community follow-up portal), never announced as discoveries.
exominer_note: NASA's ExoMiner++ is an open-source deep-learning classifier trained on Kepler and TESS data. In January 2026 NASA Ames reported it identified about 7,000 TESS planet candidates, with false-positive rejection built in. It sets the bar. This project is not a competitor: it is a transparent, classical pipeline whose every result anyone can reproduce and inspect.
